record.paper_title: Observational Cosmology: caveats and open questions in the standard model
record.original_question: Where is the missing baryonic matter predicted by Big Bang baryon-density estimates, what is the nature and amount of any non-baryonic dark matter needed for Ωm around 0.3, and do galactic dark-matter haloes with the density profiles and satellite populations predicted by cold-dark-matter models actually exist on galactic scales?

evidence.quote: Stellar and cold gas in galaxies sum a baryonic matter 8+4−5% of the total amount of the Big Bang baryonic matter predictions[218], where is the rest of the baryonic material? From here stems another open question.
Which is the nature of the putative non-baryonic dark matter to achieve the current value of Ωm ≈ 0.3?

Some authors have been led to question the very existence of this dark matter on galactic scales since its evidence is weak[221, 223, 224, 225] and the predictions do not fit the observations: the halos are not cusped as predicted, the predicted angular momentum is much less than the observed one, the number of satellites around the galaxies is much less than the predictions, etc.

There is some dark matter, it is clear, but how much, and what is its nature? The success of the standard model to convert a hypothesis into a solid theory depends strongly on the answer to these open questions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
In the standard cosmological framework, Big Bang Nucleosynthesis combined with observations of light-element abundances and the cosmic microwave background predicts a total baryonic density parameter Ω_b ≈ 0.04–0.05 (in units of the critical density ρ_crit = 3H_0^2/(8πG)). Direct censuses of stars and cold gas in galaxies, however, account for only about (8 +4/−5)% of this predicted baryonic mass. Furthermore, dynamical and lensing measurements indicate a total matter density Ω_m ≈ 0.3, far exceeding Ω_b. On galactic scales, the cold dark matter (CDM) paradigm predicts: (i) halo density profiles ρ(r) with a central cusp (e.g. Navarro–Frenk–White type, ρ(r) ∝ 1/[r(r+r_s)^2]); (ii) a specific angular-momentum distribution for baryons inside such haloes; and (iii) a large number of bound substructures (satellite subhaloes) per host halo.

Address the following:

(a) Identify the physical reservoirs (phase, temperature, location) containing the baryonic mass that is predicted by Big Bang nucleosynthesis but not observed in stars and cold galactic gas, and quantify how much baryonic matter resides in each reservoir.

(b) Determine the nature (particle content, mass, interaction cross-sections) and total cosmological abundance of any non-baryonic component required to bring the matter density parameter to Ω_m ≈ 0.3.

(c) Decide whether galactic dark-matter haloes with the CDM-predicted cuspy density profile, angular-momentum content, and satellite abundance actually exist on galactic scales, reconciling these predictions with observations of rotation curves, disk angular momenta, and observed counts of satellite galaxies.
artifact.status_search_result: All three sub-questions remain open as of 2026. The "missing baryons" problem is partially addressed by detections of the warm-hot intergalactic medium (WHIM) via fast radio burst dispersion measures and X-ray absorption, but a full accounting is still debated. The particle nature of non-baryonic dark matter is unresolved: direct-detection (LZ, XENONnT), indirect, and collider searches have so far returned null results for WIMPs, and axion searches are ongoing. The small-scale CDM challenges (cusp-core, missing satellites, too-big-to-fail, angular momentum) remain actively debated, with baryonic feedback and warm/self-interacting DM proposed as solutions but no consensus reached.

status_evidence.title: The missing baryons problem and FRB dispersion measures
status_evidence.snippet: Macquart et al. census of cosmic baryons via FRBs locates a significant fraction in the diffuse intergalactic medium, but full accounting and partition remain open.
status_evidence.claim: Missing baryons problem is partially constrained but not fully solved.

status_evidence.title: Direct detection results from LZ
status_evidence.snippet: LZ reports world-leading limits on WIMP-nucleon cross sections with no detection.
status_evidence.claim: Particle nature of non-baryonic dark matter remains unknown.

status_evidence.title: Small-scale challenges to the LCDM paradigm (review)
status_evidence.snippet: Bullock & Boylan-Kolchin review cusp/core, missing satellites, and too-big-to-fail problems and possible resolutions; debate is ongoing.
